commentary.bottom_line: Four of six hazard studies found that model discrimination, calibration, or segmentation accuracy declined over time or after protocol changes, but only two offline benchmarks tested monitoring or revalidation itself, and neither measured patient outcomes. Health systems may reasonably schedule local revalidation on the basis of the hazard evidence and 27 endorsements, while treating the method, interval, and sample size as unsettled.

perspectives.view: Two studies tested the practice, and both were level 5 offline automated benchmarks. One reported that forecasting performance improved by 38% with MLOps. The other found control-chart monitoring feasible, but in many cases it needed more than 18 validation cases. Neither was randomized or measured clinical outcomes, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

Across four deployed systems, calibration slope fell by a mean of 0.14 by nine months while AUROC declined by 0.01 to 0.03. This suggests that checks limited to discrimination may miss drift. In another study, whole gland Dice fell from 99.46% to 91.24% after an acquisition protocol change, which periodic local checks may detect.

Declines were uneven across settings. One model's AUROC fell from 0.84 to 0.73 in a U.S. dataset of 851,499 discharges, while a CT phantom study found stable results over fifteen months. Adding recent training data did not necessarily raise performance, which suggests that revalidation triggered by workflow changes may matter as much as fixed schedules.

The Duke commentary proposes performance assessment at least twice a year, but no study reports staffing or cost. The control-chart study found that 18 validation cases were often too few to accept or reject a hypothesis. This suggests that local revalidation may require case volumes that smaller sites cannot readily assemble.

Neither test of the practice reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A Canadian hazard study with a racial and ethnic minority focus found that AUROC fell from 0.737 in 2021 to 0.670 in 2022. That study did not examine whether revalidation corrected the decline for any subgroup.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployed models with and without scheduled local revalidation on patient outcomes, rates of undetected drift, or cost. Prospective studies should test revalidation intervals, minimum sample sizes, and triggers such as acquisition protocol changes. They should report calibration alongside discrimination and include subgroup results for underserved populations.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither of the two studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. They drew on a Turkish pediatric emergency department dataset and a UK sample of 318 patients. Whether local revalidation detects drift that affects these groups remains untested, and small subgroup sizes may make such detection harder at a single site.
